nameStory: Stowe's Bolas Spider gets its name from its incredible hunting technique - it spins a single sticky thread with a glue ball at the end, like the weighted weapon called a bolas used by South American gauchos. The spider whirls this "lasso" to catch flying moths, making it one of nature's most skilled hunters. The species name honors the researcher who first studied these remarkable arachnids.
description: Stowe's Bolas Spider is a chunky, rounded spider that looks almost like a small brown marble with legs. Females can reach about half an inch across, while males are much smaller and rarely seen. Instead of building traditional webs, these spiders are master chemists that create fake moth pheromones to lure their prey close enough to snag with their sticky hunting ball. They're incredibly rare in New England, with only one confirmed sighting.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely round, bulbous abdomen that feels firm and marble-like, often wider than it is long with a glossy appearance

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Hangs motionless on a single thread at night, occasionally swinging a sticky ball on a line to catch moths - no traditional web present

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Mottled brown and tan coloration with darker patches that feel slightly rough to the touch, resembling tree bark

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Females about 12-15mm (half inch) across including the swollen abdomen, with relatively short, sturdy legs

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No web structure - only a single vertical dragline thread that feels slightly tacky, with the spider hanging beneath

habitat: **[UNCERTAIN CLAIM]** Likely found in mixed deciduous forests and woodland edges where moths are abundant, particularly areas with oak and maple trees. May prefer locations near stream corridors or forest clearings where air currents help disperse their chemical lures. Given the extreme rarity, specific habitat preferences in New England remain largely unknown.

seasonality.spring: Adults likely emerge and begin establishing territories. Mating probably occurs during this period, though observations are too rare to confirm timing.
seasonality.summer: Peak hunting season when moths are most active. Females hang from branches at night, releasing pheromones and swinging their bolas to catch prey.
seasonality.fall: **[UNCERTAIN CLAIM]** Egg-laying period likely occurs, with females creating protective egg sacs before dying with the first frost.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off and the species overwinters as eggs or early instars in protected locations like bark crevices or leaf litter.

funFact: Bolas spiders are master perfumers - each species creates a unique cocktail of fake moth pheromones that perfectly mimics the "come hither" scent of female moths, essentially catfishing male moths to their doom!
confusionNotes: The extremely round abdomen makes this spider nearly impossible to confuse with any other New England species. The closest might be a gravid (egg-heavy) orb weaver, but those still build traditional webs and lack the marble-like firmness and hunting behavior.
contextualKnowledge: Bolas spiders represent one of evolution's most dramatic departures from typical spider behavior - they've completely abandoned web-building for chemical warfare and precision hunting. The extreme rarity in New England suggests this species may be at the northern edge of its range.
compareHints: **[UNCERTAIN CLAIM]** Stowe's Bolas Spider likely differs from other Mastophora species primarily in its geographic range and possibly the specific moth pheromones it produces. All bolas spiders share the same distinctive round body shape and hunting technique, making field identification to species level extremely difficult without expert analysis of their chemical signatures.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Toadlike Bolas Spider can be distinguished from other Mastophora species primarily by its particularly warty, toad-like appearance and geographic range.
Among the bolas spiders, Yeargan's species is distinguished from its relatives primarily by geographic range and subtle differences in body proportions and coloration that require expert examination.
Among the bolas spider relatives, Mastophora bisaccata is distinguished by specific details in body structure and genetic markers that require expert identification.

Among the American bolas spiders, the Cornfield Bolas Spider is distinguished by its northern range extension into New England, while most relatives like the Toadlike Bolas Spider are found in more southern regions.
Mastophora timuqua differs from its bolas spider relatives primarily in geographic distribution, as most other Mastophora species are found further south and west.
